title: Vincent of Saragossa (22 January)
hookLine: a deacon-martyr of Spain who spoke for his bishop, honored by vine-growers
tomorrow: Francis de Sales, patron of writers (24 January)

lines: A BISHOP AND HIS DEACON, ON TRIAL.
cards: Two prisoners stand before a Roman governor in Spain. One is old, a bishop, Valerius of Saragossa. The other is young, his deacon, Vincent.
The governor asks his questions, and the bishop, the story says, struggles to get the words out. So the deacon asks permission to answer for them both.
He speaks clearly and without fear, and the governor's patience snaps. The bishop is sent into exile. The deacon is kept back for something worse.

teach.b: Vincent's story comes to us in poems and sermons of the early Church. The Christian poet Prudentius wrote a long hymn to him, and Augustine of Hippo preached on his feast. Start with what he was: a deacon.
Behind that word is the Greek diakonos, a servant, someone who waits on others.
In the Acts of the Apostles, the apostles choose seven men to serve the community's tables so that widows aren't forgotten, and Catholics see there the root of the job.
Deacons serve the poor, read the Gospel at Mass, preach, and assist the bishop. Vincent served his bishop in a very literal way: as his voice. After the trial, the story is grim.
Vincent was tortured, stretched and burned, and thrown into a cell on broken pottery.

teach.h: A DARK CELL FILLS WITH LIGHT.
teach.b: There, Prudentius sings, the dark cell filled with light, the shards turned soft as flowers, and the jailer was converted. Vincent died of his wounds, a deacon-martyr of Spain. Then the vines.
In wine country, vine-growers took Vincent as their patron. People give different reasons, some half a joke about his name.

teach.h: WINTER VINES, BLESSED IN HIS NAME.
teach.b: His day falls in the dead of winter, when the vines are bare and pruning begins, and in some villages growers still walk out to bless the vines in his name. Some readers hear his feast in John's Gospel.

teach.h: I AM THE VINE: YOU THE BRANCHES.
teach.b: Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the vine: you the branches". In the same chapter, the branches that bear fruit are pruned so they bear more. Winter work, on Vincent's day.

how: Catholics keep Saint Vincent's day in January, and in some wine regions growers mark it with a Mass and a blessing of the vines.

games.q: Vincent of Saragossa — tap the pairs.
p: the poet who wrote his hymn

s: he was a deacon. the bishop was Valerius, whom he spoke for at trial.
in Prudentius's hymn, Vincent's dark cell fills with light
the shards turn soft, and the jailer is converted.
Vincent was sent into exile with his bishop
Valerius was exiled; Vincent was kept back, tortured, and died.

games.q: you're Vincent, on trial beside your bishop. he's struggling to get his words out in front of the governor. what do you do?
o: stay silent and let him speak for himself.
ask his permission to answer for you both.
plead with the governor for mercy.
games.why: in the story he asks leave to answer for both, and speaks without fear. the bishop is exiled; Vincent is tortured.

practice: Find a living plant near you, a houseplant, herbs on a sill, a tree outside the window, or bring one to mind, and look closely at the stems, the new growth, the dead leaves.
Pick one dead leaf off gently, the way a vine-grower prunes in winter. If you pray, make the sign of the cross over it and ask God's blessing; if not, give it water and a moment of attention.

wordCard.voice: Diakonos, Greek for a servant, the word behind deacon. Vincent of Saragossa was one: he spoke for his bishop at trial, died a martyr, and is honored by vine-growers in the middle of winter.

orig.note: Greek: a servant, one who waits on others; the word behind deacon.
